\chapter{Six to Ten, and the Pairs That Shaped Each Other}
\label{ch:ru-count-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{24}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count aloud from one to ten in Russian and say why vosem ends like sem and devyat begins like desyat.}

Five more numbers with no new letter, two pairs shaped by standing next to each other, and the whole run of ten scored shuffled rather than recited.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[shest]{\ru{шесть} — six}

\label{lesson:RU-C24-shest}



\begin{quote}
Count one to five, then five to one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{шесть}} — \emph{shest} — \textbf{six}
\end{quote}

One syllable, ending like \textbf{\ru{пять}} in the soft sign.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{шесть}} continues Indo-European *\emph{swé\'{k}s}, \textquotedblleft{}six.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{six}, Latin \textbf{sex} and Greek \textbf{héx} are the same word.

Notice what survived: the \emph{s}. Hold on to it, because the very last number in this slice is where that \emph{s} turns into the fact that names half the Indo-European family.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{шесть}} — six
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{\ru{шесть}} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{swé\'{k}s} $\to$ English \textbf{six}, Latin \textbf{sex}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{\ru{четыре}, \ru{пять}, \ru{шесть}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D1\%88\%D0\%B5\%D1\%81\%D1\%82\%D1\%8C}{Wiktionary: \ru{шесть}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sem]{\ru{семь} — seven}

\label{lesson:RU-C24-sem}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ru{шесть}} and its Latin cousin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{семь}} — \emph{sem} — \textbf{seven}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{семь}} continues Indo-European *\emph{septm}, \textquotedblleft{}seven.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{septem}, English \textbf{seven}, Greek \textbf{heptá} and Sanskrit \textbf{saptá} are the same word.

The \emph{p} has gone and the \emph{s} has stayed. That combination is worth marking, because the Iranian branch did the opposite: Persian's seven is \textbf{haft}, from the same word, with the \emph{s} turned into an \emph{h}. Two branches, one word, and each kept the piece the other lost.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{семь}} — seven
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{\ru{семь}} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{septm} $\to$ Latin \textbf{septem}, English \textbf{seven}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{\ru{пять}, \ru{шесть}, \ru{семь}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D1\%81\%D0\%B5\%D0\%BC\%D1\%8C}{Wiktionary: \ru{семь}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vósem]{\ru{восемь} — eight, and the seven inside it}

\label{lesson:RU-C24-vosem}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ru{семь}}, and which sound it lost that Latin kept.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{восемь}} — \emph{vósem} — \textbf{eight}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\ru{семь}} and \textbf{\ru{восемь}} one after the other. Seven is audible at the end of eight, and the unstressed \textbf{\ru{о}} at the front reduces towards \emph{a} — the reduction this book named long ago.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{восемь}} continues Indo-European *\emph{o\'{k}t\'{\={o}}w}, \textquotedblleft{}eight\textquotedblright{} — Latin \textbf{octō}, Greek \textbf{okt\'{\={o}}}, English \textbf{eight}.

There is no \emph{s} and no \emph{m} anywhere in that history, so neither is inherited. They came from \textbf{\ru{семь}}, standing next to it. Seven and eight are said together more often than almost any other pair of words in any language, and the pair pulls each other into shape: Persian's \textbf{hasht} borrowed its \emph{h}- from \textbf{haft} for exactly the same reason, in a different family, with no contact between them.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{восемь}} — eight
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{\ru{восемь}} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{o\'{k}t\'{\={o}}w} $\to$ Latin \textbf{octō}, English \textbf{eight}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{\ru{шесть}, \ru{семь}, \ru{восемь}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D0\%B2\%D0\%BE\%D1\%81\%D0\%B5\%D0\%BC\%D1\%8C}{Wiktionary: \ru{восемь}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dévyat]{\ru{девять} — nine}

\label{lesson:RU-C24-devyat}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ru{восемь}}, and where its ending came from.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{девять}} — \emph{dévyat} — \textbf{nine}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{девять}} continues Indo-European *\emph{h1newn}, \textquotedblleft{}nine.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{novem}, English \textbf{nine} and Greek \textbf{ennéa} are the same word; the \emph{n} at the front became a \emph{d} in Slavic.

That change is not an accident either, and the next lesson is the reason: \textbf{ten} begins with a \emph{d} in every branch, and \textbf{nine} stands directly in front of it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{девять}} — nine
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{\ru{девять}} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{h1newn} $\to$ Latin \textbf{novem}, English \textbf{nine}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{\ru{семь}, \ru{восемь}, \ru{девять}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D0\%B4\%D0\%B5\%D0\%B2\%D1\%8F\%D1\%82\%D1\%8C}{Wiktionary: \ru{девять}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[désyat]{\ru{десять} — ten, and the letter nine borrowed}

\label{lesson:RU-C24-desyat}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ru{девять}} and which sound changed at its front.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{десять}} — \emph{désyat} — \textbf{ten}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\ru{девять}} and \textbf{\ru{десять}} back to back. They differ in one consonant in the middle and nothing else, which makes them the pair this whole run is likeliest to confuse — so drill them together rather than in order.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{десять}} continues Indo-European *\emph{dekm}, \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{decem} — and through it \textbf{decimal}, \textbf{December}, \textbf{decade} — English \textbf{ten} and Greek \textbf{déka} are the same word.

The \emph{d} here is the original one. \textbf{\ru{девять}} copied it: nine stands in front of ten in every count anybody has ever said aloud, and it took its neighbour's first consonant, exactly as \textbf{\ru{восемь}} took its ending from \textbf{\ru{семь}} two lessons ago. Two of the last four numbers in this chapter were shaped by the number standing beside them, which is what counting aloud does to words.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{десять}} — ten
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{\ru{десять}} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{dekm} $\to$ Latin \textbf{decem}, English \textbf{ten}
  \item \emph{Pair:} \textbf{\ru{девять}} and \textbf{\ru{десять}}, one consonant apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D0\%B4\%D0\%B5\%D1\%81\%D1\%8F\%D1\%82\%D1\%8C}{Wiktionary: \ru{десять}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — one to ten}

\label{lesson:RU-C24-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count one to five, then ask \textbf{\ru{сколько}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Count aloud one to ten without a model, then ten to one.
  \item Hear all ten named singly and out of order, and say each.
  \item Read the ten printed shuffled and say each.
  \item Write all ten from dictation. Not one new Cyrillic letter appears in any of them — this whole slice adds no sign to the alphabet.
  \item Drill the two pairs that shaped each other: \textbf{\ru{семь} / \ru{восемь}}, where eight took seven's ending, and \textbf{\ru{девять} / \ru{десять}}, where nine took ten's \emph{d}.
  \item Answer \textbf{\ru{сколько}?} ten times, once with each number.
\end{enumerate}

Then say the English cousin of each. All ten have one.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
